analysis.investment_thesis: B.R. Goyal offers a reasonable earnings yield (EBIT 43 Cr / EV ~340 Cr ≈ 12.6%) but mediocre return on capital (~13-18%), which fails the Magic Formula's "cheap AND good" double test. Civil construction is inherently capital-intensive with weak FCF conversion (FY25 FCF -58 Cr), making it a pass at this stage.
key_strengths: Earnings yield ~12-13% is on the attractive threshold (P/E 8.4)
Net profit CAGR 25.6% (2020→2025); EBIT expanding 17.7% CAGR
Promoter holding 73.6% and equity doubled via FY25 capital raise (127→245 Cr)
key_risks: ROCE 17.9% is below Magic Formula's 25%+ bar — not a high-return business
FY25 Operating CF -36 Cr and FCF -58 Cr — working capital is swallowing profits
Cyclical, contract-dependent civil construction with thin 8% operating margins
red_flags: Negative OCF in FY25 despite record reported profit suggests earnings quality issues
Total assets jumped 239→440 Cr in one year (likely IPO proceeds + receivables build)
analysis.detailed_analysis: Running the Magic Formula: EBIT of ~43 Cr against an enterprise value of ~340 Cr (market cap 270 + debt 77 - minimal cash) yields an earnings yield of roughly 12.6% — just at my attractive threshold. However, return on capital is the weaker leg: on capital employed of ~322 Cr (equity 245 + debt 77), EBIT/Capital ≈ 13%, and even the company's reported ROCE of 17.9% sits well below the 25%+ I want to see. This is a cheap-ish company, but not a "good" business in the Magic Formula sense.\n\nThe deeper concern is the divergence between reported profit (25 Cr in FY25) and cash generation (OCF -36 Cr, FCF -58 Cr). Civil construction works on long receivable cycles and retention money, so the FY25 capital raise (reserves 118→221 Cr) essentially funded working capital, not growth investment. Historically FCF has been erratic (0, 26, 25, 0, -58 over 5 years). For a systematic Magic Formula buyer, this ranks as a middling candidate — I'd pass unless it cleared both screens more convincingly.
